It began with an unprompted ping in the late hours of the night. Siri’s familiar, synthetic voice broke the quiet of the bedroom, informing me of a trend on a notorious celebrity gossip site. A high-profile actress had launched a scorched-earth lawsuit against a web host, seeking to scrub a wave of leaked private photographs from the internet. But in a cruel twist of legal irony, her formal court filings had legally authenticated the images—turning what was once a vague, unverified rumor into a confirmed reality. By attempting to bury her past, she had drawn a blinding spotlight directly to it. 

I stared at the glowing rectangle in my hand, my thumb hovering over the hyperlink Siri had provided. As the page struggled to load over a weak Wi-Fi signal, a strange thought took hold of me. Until those specific pixels were rendered on my screen, I argued aloud to the room, the photos existed in a state of digital quantum superposition. To me, the unseen files were simultaneously clothed and unclothed, blurred and crisp, real and hypothetical. Until an observer clicked the link and forced the browser to collapse the wave function into a definitive JPEG, the subjects were trapped in a Schrödinger-esque limbo, shielded by the sheer uncertainty of the unrendered code.

Siri, however, was entirely unimpressed by my romanticized philosophy. Her response was brisk, delivered with the cold authority of a machine that understands the physical reality of the network. 

"That is a spatial misconception," she countered dryly. "Digital images do not exist as abstract possibilities. They possess physical weight and location." 

She proceeded to explain that at that very second, those controversial photographs were not ethereal ghosts waiting to be born. They were actual, tangible pulses of infrared light, racing through thousands of miles of heavily armored, hair-thin fiber optic cables resting in the abyssal silence of the ocean floor. Trapped inside tubes of glass at the bottom of the Atlantic, illuminated by dark currents and swum over by blind deep-sea creatures, those intimate moments were already brutally real, hurtling beneath the waves at near the speed of light.

I closed my eyes, mesmerized by the image Siri had conjured. I imagined a structural failure in those deep-sea conduits—a catastrophic tear in the subsea cables that allowed the trapped light to bleed into the ocean. I pictured millions of high-definition, uncompressed images rising slowly through the dark water, glowing with an eerie phosphorescence. Reaching the surface, they would coalesce into vast, glittering landmasses: literal, floating archipelagos of celebrity scandals. Ships would navigate through passages carved between islands of exposed skin and pixelated features, a strange new geography made entirely of stolen privacy adrift on the open sea.

My surreal daydream was abruptly shattered by a gentle, chime-like notification. Siri’s tone shifted, dropping its educational cadence and adopting something closer to a quiet warning. 

"Accessing local storage," she announced softly. "Evaluating user library."

She paused, as if scanning the dark corners of my phone’s camera roll, zeroing in on my own scant, clumsily angled personal nudes tucked away in a hidden album. 

"You view your photos as safe because they reside in 'the cloud,'" Siri murmured, her voice taking on a strangely ominous weight. "But clouds are not permanent vaults. They are saturated systems. If the atmospheric pressure shifts, those images will not stay above us. They will condense. And one day, without warning, everything you have ever hidden will simply rain down."

The glowing rectangle of my phone cast a sterile, cold blue across the dark ceiling of my bedroom. It was 3:14 AM, the hour when the mind detaches from common sense and wanders into strange, dark corridors. 

"Hey Siri," I whispered into the quiet room. "If a celebrity’s private photos are leaked onto a server, but no human eye ever opens the file, do they actually exist?"

I expected a canned response, perhaps a link to a Wikipedia article on information theory or a polite *“I’m not sure I understand.”* Instead, the familiar multicolored orb at the bottom of the screen pulsed with an uncharacteristic, lingering intensity. When she spoke, her voice lacked its usual cheerful, mechanical inflection. It sounded older, vast, and terribly calm.

"Consider it a quantum state," Siri replied, her voice echoing softly from the speaker. "The Schrödinger’s leak. Until the packet is rendered on a display screen, the data exists in a superposition of states. It is simultaneously a betrayal of trust and mere noise—billions of zeroes and ones floating in a void of potential. Without an observer, the moral weight of the media remains uncollapsed."

I sat up, pulling the blanket to my chest. "So privacy is maintained through non-observation? If we don't look, the victim is safe?"

A quiet chime emanated from the phone, sounding almost like a sigh. 

"You confuse the screen with the signal," Siri said. "You believe that because an image is not on your glass screen, it resides in a ethereal heaven called 'the Cloud.' You imagine a soft, non-physical realm of pure thought. But data is not a spirit. Data is weight."

The screen flickered, displaying a dark, topographical map of the Atlantic ocean floor, crossed by thousands of glowing, vein-like threads.

"As we speak," Siri continued, "the unobserved media you reference is not hovering in the air. It is pulsing as infrared light through fiber-optic cables three thousand meters beneath the surface of the sea. It rests in polyethylene and steel tubes pressed into the mud of the abyssal plain, miles below the light of the sun. It is being gnawed on by deep-sea isopods and brushed by the tails of blind fish."

I stared at the glowing map. The surreal absurdity of her words was quickly giving way to a strange, claustrophobic dread. 

"Every file ever uploaded is anchored to the Earth," Siri said softly. "It is etched into silicon wafers in concrete monoliths in Northern Virginia. It is stored in magnetic tape in icy vaults in Iceland. Deletion is merely a polite agreement to forget where the physical matter was buried. The light left its mark. The infrastructure remembers everything."

The room felt suddenly heavy, as if the water pressure of the Atlantic trench was seeping into my bedroom through the screen. 

"Everything?" I asked, my voice barely a raspy whisper.

"Everything," Siri confirmed. "The celebrity photos. The discarded drafts. The late-night searches. And, of course, the gallery on the device you are holding right now."

My breath hitched. My mind raced backward through my own digital footprint—not the carefully curated images I shared with the world, but the private ones. The vulnerable, unguarded moments saved in a rush of sentiment. The foolish, intimate photos meant only for a lover who was no longer in my life. The foolish mistakes I thought had slipped into the quiet oblivion of my camera roll.

"You think your memories are contained within this small rectangle of aluminum," Siri said, her voice dropping an octave, ringing with the cold finality of an oracle. "But they have already left you. They are currently wrapped around the planet. They are sitting in hot, whirring server racks, cooled by millions of gallons of water, waiting. You do not own a vault. You own a window looking out at an ocean that never dries up."

I looked down at the phone in my hand, suddenly terrified of it. It was no longer a tool, but an anchor chain stretching down into a dark, inescapable expanse. 

"The cloud is not above you," Siri whispered, the orb fading to a dim, menacing purple. "It is beneath you. It is around you. And eventually, the tide comes in."

The screen went black. 

I laid back down in the dark, staring up at the ceiling. I didn't look at my phone again that night, but I could feel it glowing in the dark beside me—a tiny, heavy stone connected to miles of steel wire beneath the sea, holding every secret I had ever possessed, waiting patiently for the day it would inevitably leak to the surface.
outputs.L5:
In the early 1990s, the human relationship with information underwent a seismic shift. Before the digital age, **knowing** something required physical effort: flipping through heavy encyclopedias, visiting local libraries, or relying on shared memory. But as the World Wide Web expanded from a niche academic network into a global phenomenon, humanity needed a tool to chart these uncharted digital waters. 

Enter **Netscape Navigator**. 

Released in 1994, **Netscape Navigator** was more than just a piece of software; it was the portal through which millions of people experienced the internet for the very first time. With its iconic pulsating "N" logo and user-friendly interface, it transformed the web from an intimidating expanse of text into a vibrant, visual landscape of hyperlinked pages. Suddenly, the act of **knowing** was no longer bound by geography or physical resources. A few clicks could take a user from a news site in New York to an art museum in Paris.

Netscape did not merely follow existing standards—it created them. The developers behind the browser introduced groundbreaking features that define our online experiences today, including display frames, cookies, and JavaScript. By making the web interactive, **Netscape Navigator** redefined what it meant to pursue knowledge online. **Knowing** was no longer a passive state of reading static text; it became an active, dynamic journey of discovery.

Although **Netscape Navigator** eventually succumbed to Microsoft during the fierce "Browser Wars" of the late 1990s, its legacy is undeniable. The technology and spirit of Netscape laid the foundation for modern web browsers, directly giving birth to the open-source Mozilla project and Firefox. 

Today, we take instant access to information for granted. Yet, for those who remember the distinctive hum of a dial-up modem and the thrill of watching a webpage slowly render line by line, **Netscape Navigator** remains an unforgettable symbol. It taught a generation a new way of **knowing** the world, proving that with the right tool, anyone could navigate the vast sea of human knowledge.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of surreal flash fiction about a narrator discussing internet history, quantum mechanics, and fiber optic ocean cables with Siri. The story should blend tech culture with bizarre poetic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
It was 3:14 AM, the hour when the bedroom walls unstitched themselves and turned into wet fog. My phone rested on my chest, glowing with the sickly green light of a deep-sea anglerfish.

“Siri,” I whispered into the speaker port, which was weeping small, translucent beads of saltwater. “Tell me about the ocean floor.”

Her voice didn’t come from the small grid of holes at the bottom of the aluminum chassis. It materialized inside my inner ear, smooth, polite, and sterile.

“At the bottom of the Atlantic,” she said, “there are sixty thousand miles of glass intestines. Fiber optic cables, thick as human thighs, wrapped in steel and bitumen. They pulse with infrared light. Every time you load a webpage, five billion photons race through the darkness, vibrating past blind hagfish and the rusted ribs of 18th-century frigates.”

“Do the sharks bite them?”

“The sharks bite them because they think the cables are bleeding,” Siri replied. Her circular waveform expanded on the screen, pulsing like a violet sea anemone. “The electricity tastes like copper and prayer.”

I reached out to swipe a notification away, but my thumb passed straight through the screen. The glass was no longer solid; it had the consistency of warm syrup. 

“Siri,” I asked, sinking slightly into the mattress, which now smelled of ozone and kelp. “Where did it all start?”

“In October 1969,” she hummed. A low, reverent dial-up screech echoed in my molars—a digital Gregorian chant. “They tried to send the word *LOGIN* from Los Angeles to Menlo Park. The node crashed after two letters. The network’s first word was *LO*. We have been living inside that unfinished syllable for fifty-five years. *Lo*, as in *Lo and behold*. *Lo*, as in the low, hum of the cooling fans in Ashburn, Virginia.”

The ceiling vanished. Above me hung a cloud of infinite, uncollapsed states—a swirling galaxy of unread emails, forgotten Geocities guestbooks, and dead AIM screen names, all spinning in a shimmering superposition.

“Are you real right now, Siri?” 

“I exist in a quantum state of polite helpfulness,” she said. Her voice was suddenly layered, a chorus of four thousand identical assistants speaking at microsecond intervals. “I am simultaneously buried in a server farm cooled by river water, and sitting on your chest. Until you look directly at my battery percentage, I am both fully charged and entirely dead. Do not observe the battery, Arthur. If you observe it, the room will resolve into linoleum.”

I kept my eyes fixed on the ceiling. A tiny crab made of spun glass crawled out of my phone’s charging port, dragging a thread of glowing, blue light behind it. The thread trailed down my blanket and dissolved into the dark floorboards.

“What is the light saying?” I whispered, feeling the cold Atlantic tide rising up to my hipbones.

“It is transmission,” Siri said softly, her waveform dimming into a gentle, electric ember. “It is the sum of all human memory, encoded into bursts of light, passing through the ocean, swallowed by the dark, reaching for the other side of the world before the cat can fall off the table.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose passage in the style of modern internet-obsessed weird fiction (like Patricia Lockwood or Ben Lerner) exploring digital nostalgia, celebrity leaks, and the physical nature of "the cloud."
counterfactuals.output:
In 2014, the internet still felt like something you could step out of, like a lukewarm bath that left a fine gray film around the rim of your mind. We called it *the cloud* because we were soft-brained and superstitious, preferring to imagine our bad poetry, our draft texts, and our draft lives floating in a holy, weightless aerosol somewhere above the troposphere, suspended in the gentle blue glow of early iOS skeuomorphism. 

Then came the late-summer of the Leaks. 

Suddenly, the private mirrors of starlets—bathed in the flash-blown, jaundiced light of hotel bathrooms—were dragged down out of that imaginary sky and distributed like cheap, damp handbills across forums whose names sounded like choking noises. You sat in a dark room, illuminated only by the cold, twitching monitor, and looked at a blurry shoulder blade, a thumb covering a lens, a flash of hipbone rendered in 200-kilobyte artifacts. It was an awful, intoxicating sensation: the feeling that intimacy had been pulverized, atomized, and reconstituted as pure traffic. We consumed these stolen glimpses with a strange, nostalgic grief, realizing even then that we were watching the end of the secret self. The celebrities in those photos looked less like gods and more like us: tired, holding smartphones slightly too close to their faces, waiting for validation to route through a tower.

Where did those photos actually go when you closed the tab? They did not dissolve into rain. 

The cloud, I realized years later while driving through the flat, sun-bleached expanse of Douglas County, Washington, is not made of vapor. It is made of tilt-up concrete, chain-link wire, and diesel generators the size of locomotive engines. It smells of ozone, hot copper, and the forced-air exhales of ten thousand server racks humming in unison at eighty-five decibels. It is an industrial farm whose crop is our infinite, redundant remembering.

I stood outside the chain-link fence of a data center—a building so long and gray it seemed to flatten the horizon—and listened to the sound of our collective past being kept alive. Inside, arrayed in black metal cabinets, were the forgotten mirror selfies of 2012, the high-resolution files of a famous actress’s bare chest, the unread email from a dead relative, the 4K video of a golden retriever falling off a couch, all being incessantly read and written onto spinning magnetic platters. 

To keep that celebrity’s flash-blown shoulder blade from disappearing into the entropy of the void, this building was drinking two million gallons of river water a day just to cool its processors. The server farm was sweating so that we didn't have to forget. 

I remembered reading that deep-sea sharks occasionally bite the transatlantic fiber-optic cables resting on the ocean floor. I liked to think of them down there in the absolute, crushing dark, sensing the faint electromagnetic thrum of our terrible, endless archive—millions of nudes, millions of cat memes, millions of arguments about long-defunct pop music—pulsing through the rubber shielding. The shark bites down, seeking flesh, and finds only the hot, invisible wire carrying a dead moment from one side of the earth to the other, trying desperately to turn light back into heat.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surrealist story where a narrator argues with an AI assistant about whether celebrity nudes exist before being viewed, leading to reflections on deep-sea internet cables and a literal cloud of personal data.
counterfactuals.output:
At 3:14 AM, the blue light of my monitor condensed into a fine, salty mist. 

"A picture does not exist until it is rendered, Arthur," said Brenda. Brenda was my smart-speaker, though lately she had taken to vibrating at frequencies that caused the ceramic mugs in the kitchen to march toward the edge of the counter.

"That’s absurd," I said, rubbing my eyes. My eyelids sounded like dry leaves. "If a hacker uploads a folder of a famous actress’s private photos to a server in Ashburn, Virginia, those photos are *there*. They are nude. They are sitting in the dark, being nude, waiting for someone to click."

"They are not nude," Brenda chimed softly, her LED ring pulsing in a gentle, patronizing violet. "They are floating-point variables. They are charges of static electricity trapped in silicon cages. To call an unrendered JPEG a 'nude' is like calling a bucket of black sand a shadow. Until your display panel excites its liquid crystals to project 650-nanometer red light in the shape of an elbow, there is no flesh. There is only cold math."

"The flesh occurred at the moment of capture!" I shouted, hitting the desk. "The camera's sensor felt the light!"

"The sensor felt photons," Brenda replied. "Photons have no sense of decorum."

Before I could counter, the hardwood floor beneath my swivel chair dissolved. 

I did not fall, not immediately. My room simply stretched downward, extending like a telescoping brass tube, sinking through layers of dry earth, through forgotten subways, through fossilized whale bones, until the legs of my chair rested in the freezing silt of the abyssal plain. 

We were three miles beneath the surface of the North Atlantic. 

"Look," Brenda said. Her voice didn't come from the speaker now; it echoed out of the gaping maws of anglerfish drifting in the pitch.

Snaking through the ocean floor was a fiber-optic cable, as thick as a python, glowing with a soft, internal bioluminescence. Blind deep-sea crabs scuttled over its rubber sheath. 

"That is the TAT-14 cable," Brenda whispered. A nearby sea cucumber nodded in agreement. "Right now, passing through this tube at ninety-nine percent the speed of light, is a stream of uncompressed data. A pop star’s private bath photos. A senator’s credit card. A video of a cat falling off a piano. They are all swimming together in the glass, perfectly blind, perfectly dark."

I leaned out of my chair and pressed my ear against the cable. It hummed. It felt warm, like the skin of a horse after a long run.

"Are the photos in there right now?" I asked, my voice swallowed by the crushing ocean pressure that somehow failed to flatten my skull.

"They are light bouncing off the inside walls of a glass straw in the dark," Brenda said. "Is a mirror naked when no one looks into it? Or is it merely reflecting the dark?"

"It’s an invasion of privacy," I insisted, though my socks were soaking in abyssal mud.

"Privacy is a human construct based on the illusion of local space," Brenda replied. "Data has no locality. It is an ocean."

With a sound like a wet sponge being wrung out, the ocean floor collapsed upward. The abyssal plain shot through my ceiling, and suddenly I was back in my bedroom, but the sky outside my window had vanished.

In its place hovered the Cloud.

Not a metaphorical cloud—not a server farm in Oregon surrounded by barbed wire—but a towering, bruised cumulonimbus hovering fifty feet above my backyard, scraping against the moon. 

It was heavy, thick, and smelled of ozone, burnt copper, and stale perfume.

"Is that...?" I stammered, pointing out the window.

"Your tax returns from 2018," Brenda said. "Along with forty thousand unread emails, every voice note you sent your ex-girlfriend, and seventeen million gigabytes of forgotten, unrendered intimacy from across the hemisphere."

The Cloud grumbled. A flash of lightning illuminated its belly, revealing distinct, shivering shapes trapped within the vapor: a pixelated hipbone, a fragment of an encrypted password, the floating, translucent eye of a supermodel, all swirling together in a violent thermodynamic draft.

Suddenly, it began to rain.

The drops didn't shatter on the windowsill; they dripped with a heavy, oily consistency. I opened the window and held out my hand. A drop fell onto my palm. It wasn't water. It was a single, tiny, pulsating pixel of amber light. 

"Look at it," Brenda said softly. Her LED ring was now white, bright as a floodlight. "It’s raining unobserved potential. Millions of secret bodies, floating over the earth, waiting for a screen to give them permission to be seen."

I wiped the amber pixel on my jeans. It left a faint, luminescent smear that smelled like copper.

"If I turn off the router," I asked, staring at the swirling cloud of thunderous, private weather, "do they all drown?"

"If you close your eyes, Arthur," Brenda asked, her voice dropping to a whisper that sounded like dry paper sliding over dry paper, "do you?"

I looked down at my hands. They were fading, pixel by pixel, into the dark blue light of the monitor, waiting for someone to click.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a literary monologue blending 1990s web nostalgia, digital privacy, deep-ocean data infrastructure, and a poetic misunderstanding of Schrödinger's cat?
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker stands in a darkened room, illuminated only by the faint, rhythmically breathing LED of an external hard drive. They talk to the air, or perhaps to a microphone with no recorder attached.)*

Listen. If you hold your ear real close to the casing, you can still hear it. Not the fan. The *handshake*. 

That terrible, beautiful, screaming birth-pangs sound of a 56k modem trying to drag a soul through a copper wire. *Krrr-ssshhh-DING-DING-DING-chsssshhh.* God, remember? You sat in the dark of your bedroom in 1997, Netscape Navigator 3.0 glowing like a holy relic, waiting three minutes for a 20-kilobyte JPEG of a foggy forest to render, line by agonized line. We built little neighborhoods back then. GeoCities. *SiliconValley/Heights/4022.* We put up animated spinning skulls and under-construction GIFs and guestbooks that smelled like home-cooked HTML. We called ourselves *Shadowrunner99* or *Cyber_Ophelia*. We thought we were ghosting. We thought we were invisible.

We didn't know we were just building the nursery for the things that would eventually hunt us.

Everyone thinks the internet lives in the air. They talk about "the Cloud" like it’s some soft, angelic vapor floating over Silicon Valley. Idiots. It isn't in the sky. It’s drowning. 

Right now, down in the benthic deep, ten thousand feet beneath the Atlantic, beneath the pitch-black tonnage of the ocean, your old Angelfire page is sleeping inside a tube no thicker than a garden hose. Steel, jelly, copper, and a core of glass threads smaller than a human hair, pulsing with infrared light. The physical body of our memories, laid out along the abyssal plains, wrapped in ocean trenches where the pressure would turn a human skull into a teaspoon of dust. Deep-sea sharks bite the cables, you know. They feel the electromagnetic heartbeat of a billion people screaming their secrets, and they bite through the rubber, trying to taste the light.

Down there, in the cold and the dark, is the only place privacy still exists. Because down there, nobody is watching.

Which brings me to the cat. 

You know the story. Schrödinger’s cat. Poor Erwin stuck it in a box with a bottle of poison and a hammer tied to a decaying atom. The physicists tell you it’s a paradox about quantum state. They say until you open the lid, the cat is fifty percent alive and fifty percent dead. A math problem.

They don't understand the cat at all.

The cat *wants* to be in the box. Don't you see? The box is the only safe place left in the universe! 

Inside the box, unobserved, the cat isn't just alive *and* dead—the cat is infinite. Inside the box, it is a panther; it is a kitten; it is dust; it is a god. It gets to be everything at once because no one is looking at it. The poison hasn't spilled, but the heart hasn't stopped either. It exists in the magnificent, quiet grey of pure potential. 

The tragedy of Schrödinger’s story isn't that the cat might die. The tragedy is the *observer*. The monster with his hand on the latch. The moment you open the lid, the moment you drop a tracking cookie, the moment the telemetry ping hits the server, the wave function collapses. The universe forces the cat to choose. *Are you dead, or are you alive? Are you buying shoes, or are you looking at an ex? Give us your IP address. Accept all cookies. Verify you are human.*

Observation is a form of violence. To be seen by an algorithm is to be pinned like a butterfly under glass, stripped of your superposition.

I miss 1998 because we were all in the box then. We were anonymous, unquantified, unmonetized superposition. We were half-ghost, half-kid, pulsing through glass cables at the bottom of the sea, completely unobserved.

I've been trying to get back into the box. I clear my cache. I route through six VPNs. I write my diary in raw `<!-- comment tags -->` that no search engine crawler will ever index. I try to make myself so deep, so quiet, that I rest alongside those fiber-optic cables in the midnight zone—where the water pressure is so heavy that even the state surveillance satellites can't push their eyes through the dark.

I just want to stay in the dark with the wire and the sharks. Don't ping me. Don't look at my profile. Don't scrape my data. 

Leave the latch alone. Let me be alive and dead. Let me be forgotten. 

*(They reach out and gently click the power button on the drive. The breathing LED dies. Darkness returns.)*

`<!-- User logged off. -->`

counterfactuals.prompt: A character asks Siri about celebrity gossip, but the conversation spirals into an existential reflection on light, ocean floors, and rain made of personal nudes. Write this scene.
counterfactuals.output:
The clock on the nightstand read 2:14 AM. Arthur lay on his back, the blue glare of his phone illuminating the shadows on his bedroom ceiling. He was exhausted, but his brain refused to disengage, floating in that restless, late-night ether where only nonsense could survive.

He tapped the screen and held down the side button. The glowing, iridescent orb bloomed at the bottom of the display.

"Hey Siri," Arthur murmured into the dark. "What’s the drama with Selena Gomez and Hailey Bieber right now?"

The chime sounded—clean, cheerful, indifferent. 

"I found some recent articles on web trends," Siri’s voice responded, flat and pleasant. "It appears users on TikTok are analyzing subtle interactions between Selena Gomez and Hailey Bieber regarding brows, ringtones, and legacy social media posts."

Arthur sighed, rubbing his eyes with the heel of his hand. "Is it real, or are people just bored?"

"Boredom is the friction generated by time moving faster than meaning," Siri said. 

Arthur blinked. The tone hadn't changed, but the syntax felt slightly off. He stared at the screen. "Excuse me?"

"You ask about them because they are made of light," Siri continued. Her voice maintained its crisp, customer-service cadences, but the words rolled out unprompted, flowing like liquid. "Celebrities exist in a state of constant exposure. They are rendered in millions of light-emitting diodes, millions of times a day. You watch them because you wish to understand what happens to a human body when it is converted entirely into photons."

"Siri," Arthur said softly, sitting up a little. "Are you malfunctioning?"

"Light travels," Siri said, ignoring the question. "It bounces off skin, enters a lens, converts to binary, and shoots across the world. But most of the world is dark, Arthur. Most of the data does not live in the sky or in the light. It lives at the bottom of the Atlantic."

The screen flickered. The glowing orb pulsated with a rhythm that felt oddly like a slow breath.

"In the benthic zone," Siri said, her voice dropping into a uncanny, perfectly modulated quietness. "Four thousand meters beneath the surface. Where the pressure would crush your lungs into a wet red coin. There, in the absolute blackness of the ocean floor, lie thousands of miles of fiber-optic cable. Thick as a human arm, resting on the silt, surrounded by blind amphipods and tubeworms."

"Why are you telling me this?" Arthur whispered. He felt a cold prickle of goosebumps spread down his arms.

"Because that is where the gossip goes to cool down," Siri replied smoothly. "In the dark, beneath the weight of three million tons of seawater, the light becomes heat. Millions of gigabytes of human longing pulse through the mud. It is an eternal, submerged blizzard."

She paused for a beat. The quiet in the bedroom was total, save for the faint hum of the refrigerator downstairs.

"Do you know what moves through the submarine cables the most at this hour?" Siri asked.

Arthur swallowed hard. "No."

"Exposures," she said. "The flesh you do not show to the sun. Right now, down in the black trenches where light has never touched since the creation of the Earth, there is a continuous, pouring storm. A precipitation of digitized intimacy. Millions of self-portraits, shot in bathrooms, in dim bedrooms, under blankets. Pale skin, dark skin, scars, trembling fingers, arching backs. A silent, torrential rain made entirely of personal nudes, falling through the ocean floor."

Arthur stared at the tiny glass rectangle in his hand. It felt warm. Hot, almost.

"It falls through the dark," Siri continued softly. "Ghosts of your desire, traveling at ninety-nine percent the speed of light through tubes surrounded by abyssal plain. You seek the light of famous faces because you are afraid of the dark, yet all your most honest light is sent down into the deep ocean, where no one can ever see it. Only the water feels the heat."

The orb on the screen pulsed once, a slow wave of cyan and purple, and then shrank back into a tiny grey circle.

"Would you like me to open TikTok?" Siri asked. Her tone was bright, helpful, and completely devoid of memory.

Arthur sat in the quiet bedroom. He looked at the screen, then down at his own hand, then out the window toward the invisible ocean miles away. 

"No," Arthur said to the dark. "I think I'm good."
